title: The highest good is like water
hookLine: the highest good is like water: it benefits all and seeks the low places (Tao Te Ching 8)
carry: the highest good helps all and takes the low place
tomorrow: the cup, the blade and the treasure hall
last: WHAT DOESN'T LIVE FOR ITSELF LASTS.

cards: A glass tips over at dinner. In a second the water is everywhere it can reach. It runs along the grain of the table, slips under the edge of a plate, finds the one low spot by the salt shaker, and drips off the corner.
Nobody told it where to go. It didn't argue with the plate. It went around.
Water seems to know exactly where the lowest place is. Chapter eight of the Tao Te Ching looks at that and sees the highest good.

teach.b: First, it benefits all things. The highest good, the chapter opens, is like water. In Legge's translation: "The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things."
It waters the rose and the weed without sorting them first.

teach.h: IT TAKES THE PLACE NOBODY WANTS.
teach.b: Second, it takes the place nobody wants. Water settles without striving in the low places people dislike, and that, the chapter says, is why it's close to the Tao.
The valley, the one who goes last, the empty bowl: water is all of them at once.

teach.h: GOOD GROUND, DEEP HEART, RIGHT TIMING.
teach.b: Third, good ground, deep heart, right timing. Then comes a short list that's easy to skip. In a home, goodness like water is the ground it stands on.
In the heart, depth. In giving, kindness. In speech, being trustworthy.
In leading, good order. In work, ability. In action, good timing.
Ordinary virtues, the kind that show up in a kitchen or an office on a weekday. Water isn't only humble. It's useful, steady and on time.
The chapter ends on its plainest line: because water doesn't contend, no one finds fault with it. It goes around the plate, and gets where it was going anyway.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep chapter eight's opening words, the highest good is like water, written where they will see them.

o: good that helps all and takes the lowest place
always changing, never keeping a promise
weak, giving in to whoever pushes hardest

s: chapter eight compares the highest good to a mountain peak
it compares it to water, which benefits all things and settles in the low places.
chapter eight says water is close to the Tao because it takes the place people dislike
it settles without striving in the low places, and so it is near to the Tao.
its short list also praises depth, kindness, trustworthiness, order, ability and good timing.

games.q: a glass tips over and the water reaches a plate in its path. what does the water do?
o: push the plate out of the way.
games.why: it goes around. chapter eight ends: because water doesn't contend, no one finds fault with it.

practice: If you can, pour a little water slowly into a sink, a bowl or a plant, and watch where it goes: it doesn't push; it spreads, finds the low point and settles.
Then sit with your eyes on it, or on the memory of it, and let each breath settle low in your body the same way. If you pray, you can pray with the water in front of you; if not, just keep watching.

wordCard.voice: Like water. Chapter eight's picture of the highest good: it benefits all things, takes the low place nobody wants, and doesn't quarrel. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, shàng shàn ruò shuǐ: the highest good is like water. The opening of Tao Te Ching 8.
